metadata.title: JZ Mock C · Paper 2
metadata.description: Worked steps, progressive hints and reviewed follow-up questions.

matches.rationale: Both track prime exponents through powers/products and test whether a constraint on the resulting number forces the same constraint on its factors. The original fixes divisibility of one square by12; the candidate applies a supplied even-exponent theorem to products and also constructs a repairing multiplier.
sharedKnowledge: Both track prime exponents through powers/products and test whether a constraint on the resulting number forces the same constraint on its factors. The original fixes divisibility of one square by12; the candidate applies a supplied even-exponent theorem to products and also constructs a repairing multiplier.

matches.rationale: Both determine which products and quotients preserve an initial order by tracking multiplier signs. The original permits every real sign and includes squares/cubes; the candidate fixes all inputs negative and compares a chain and two ratios.
sharedKnowledge: Both determine which products and quotients preserve an initial order by tracking multiplier signs. The original permits every real sign and includes squares/cubes; the candidate fixes all inputs negative and compares a chain and two ratios.

matches.rationale: Both expand the square of a sine-plus-cosine expression and use sine squared plus cosine squared equal to one to connect the sum and product. The original then computes a symmetric cube sum; the candidate instead audits an unsquaring step and must retain a negative branch.
sharedKnowledge: Both expand the square of a sine-plus-cosine expression and use sine squared plus cosine squared equal to one to connect the sum and product. The original then computes a symmetric cube sum; the candidate instead audits an unsquaring step and must retain a negative branch.

matches.rationale: Both ask which height/derivative claims necessarily follow from polynomial monotonicity on an interval, using whole-interval counterexamples for claims not forced. The original additionally tests signed area and a midpoint comparison; the candidate additionally compares second-derivative endpoint values.
sharedKnowledge: Both ask which height/derivative claims necessarily follow from polynomial monotonicity on an interval, using whole-interval counterexamples for claims not forced. The original additionally tests signed area and a midpoint comparison; the candidate additionally compares second-derivative endpoint values.

matches.rationale: Both test implication directions involving polynomial stationary behaviour and separate a proof from an allowed polynomial counterexample. The original relates a local maximum to coefficient/derivative restrictions atzero; the candidate relates an interior horizontal tangent to equal endpoint heights, requiring an interval-extremum argument rather than a second-derivative condition.
sharedKnowledge: Both test implication directions involving polynomial stationary behaviour and separate a proof from an allowed polynomial counterexample. The original relates a local maximum to coefficient/derivative restrictions atzero; the candidate relates an interior horizontal tangent to equal endpoint heights, requiring an interval-extremum argument rather than a second-derivative condition.

matches.rationale: Both differentiate real fractional powers, factor the derivative and track its sign across the negative and positive parts of a domain excluding zero. The original audits a provided argument with a positive reciprocal of an even power of the real cube root; the candidate has an odd-root-power denominator whose sign changes at zero.
sharedKnowledge: Both differentiate real fractional powers, factor the derivative and track its sign across the negative and positive parts of a domain excluding zero. The original audits a provided argument with a positive reciprocal of an even power of the real cube root; the candidate has an odd-root-power denominator whose sign changes at zero.

matches.rationale: Both expand fractional powers, differentiate and remove a positive power prefactor before solving a quadratic sign condition. The original checks six proof lines over nonzero reals; the candidate restricts to a positive unit interval and additionally measures its decreasing fraction.
sharedKnowledge: Both expand fractional powers, differentiate and remove a positive power prefactor before solving a quadratic sign condition. The original checks six proof lines over nonzero reals; the candidate restricts to a positive unit interval and additionally measures its decreasing fraction.

matches.rationale: Both evaluate every labelled container statement at one shared integer count and enforce exactly one truth. The labels and allowed counts differ: the original includes primality, divisibility and squares on3…8; the candidate uses five interval/equality labels on all positive integers. It is a genuine variant, not a reprint.
sharedKnowledge: Both evaluate every labelled container statement at one shared integer count and enforce exactly one truth. The labels and allowed counts differ: the original includes primality, divisibility and squares on3…8; the candidate uses five interval/equality labels on all positive integers. It is a genuine variant, not a reprint.

matches.rationale: Both write a polynomial division identity and evaluate at the zero of the divisor to isolate its remainder. The candidate has a constant remainder from one linear divisor; the original uses a quadratic divisor and two evaluations to determine a linear remainder.
sharedKnowledge: Both write a polynomial division identity and evaluate at the zero of the divisor to isolate its remainder. The candidate has a constant remainder from one linear divisor; the original uses a quadratic divisor and two evaluations to determine a linear remainder.

matches.rationale: Both use evaluations at two linear-divisor zeros and subtract the resulting equations to eliminate a shared constant. The original recovers a linear remainder exactly; the candidate then maximises a remainder difference over distinct allowed coefficients.
sharedKnowledge: Both use evaluations at two linear-divisor zeros and subtract the resulting equations to eliminate a shared constant. The original recovers a linear remainder exactly; the candidate then maximises a remainder difference over distinct allowed coefficients.

matches.rationale: Both distinguish remaining answer configurations through possible feedback and prove a minimal observation count by showing ambiguity before a successful distinguishing test. The original compares the best possible truth-check outcome of four answer sets; the candidate first enumerates restricted permutations and designs feedback that guarantees identification.
sharedKnowledge: Both distinguish remaining answer configurations through possible feedback and prove a minimal observation count by showing ambiguity before a successful distinguishing test. The original compares the best possible truth-check outcome of four answer sets; the candidate first enumerates restricted permutations and designs feedback that guarantees identification.

matches.rationale: Both classify acute SSA configurations by comparing an opposite side with the perpendicular height and adjacent-side length, including tangency and a collapsed vertex. The original then tests necessary supersets for the two-triangle interval; the candidate asks for the full one-triangle set.
sharedKnowledge: Both classify acute SSA configurations by comparing an opposite side with the perpendicular height and adjacent-side length, including tangency and a collapsed vertex. The original then tests necessary supersets for the two-triangle interval; the candidate asks for the full one-triangle set.

matches.rationale: Both retain the two valid branches of one acute SSA ray/circle construction. The original classifies the parameter interval in which two triangles exist; the candidate uses a given area ratio to relate those two branches and recover the common angle.
sharedKnowledge: Both retain the two valid branches of one acute SSA ray/circle construction. The original classifies the parameter interval in which two triangles exist; the candidate uses a given area ratio to relate those two branches and recover the common angle.

matches.rationale: Both distinguish the two nondegenerate triangle configurations permitted by an acute SSA specification. The original teaches the altitude/adjacent-side inequalities to find the full two-triangle interval, then tests a necessary condition. The candidate instead calculates the two unknown-side branches using a cosine-rule quadratic and compares their areas; those calculations are additional candidate operations.
sharedKnowledge: Both distinguish the two nondegenerate triangle configurations permitted by an acute SSA specification. The original teaches the altitude/adjacent-side inequalities to find the full two-triangle interval, then tests a necessary condition. The candidate instead calculates the two unknown-side branches using a cosine-rule quadratic and compares their areas; those calculations are additional candidate operations.

matches.rationale: Both test the whole nonzero-real domain when comparing powers, odd roots and reciprocals as conditions forcing input order. The original asks for both necessity and sufficiency and uses fifth roots/two-thirds powers; the candidate asks sufficiency with three-fifths and fourth powers, so the expressions and implication demand differ.
sharedKnowledge: Both test the whole nonzero-real domain when comparing powers, odd roots and reciprocals as conditions forcing input order. The original asks for both necessity and sufficiency and uses fifth roots/two-thirds powers; the candidate asks sufficiency with three-fifths and fourth powers, so the expressions and implication demand differ.

matches.rationale: Both differentiate a parameterised cubic, use turning heights and boundary repeated roots to determine the exact one-root set, then classify an offered condition by set containment. The original asks for a necessary insufficient superset and has a merged-stationary-point special case; the candidate asks for a sufficient subset under vertical translation.
sharedKnowledge: Both differentiate a parameterised cubic, use turning heights and boundary repeated roots to determine the exact one-root set, then classify an offered condition by set containment. The original asks for a necessary insufficient superset and has a merged-stationary-point special case; the candidate asks for a sufficient subset under vertical translation.

matches.rationale: Both locate a cubic’s stationary inputs and evaluate their heights to derive a full parameter interval for a required distinct-root count. The candidate wants three roots under vertical translation; the original wants one root and then a necessary condition, also handling coincident stationary inputs.
sharedKnowledge: Both locate a cubic’s stationary inputs and evaluate their heights to derive a full parameter interval for a required distinct-root count. The candidate wants three roots under vertical translation; the original wants one root and then a necessary condition, also handling coincident stationary inputs.

matches.rationale: Both derive cubic root-count conditions from the signs of two turning heights and check equality boundaries. The candidate keeps its stationary inputs distinct through m>0 and seeks a three-root range in n; the original has a special merged case and asks a logical condition for one root.
sharedKnowledge: Both derive cubic root-count conditions from the signs of two turning heights and check equality boundaries. The candidate keeps its stationary inputs distinct through m>0 and seeks a three-root range in n; the original has a special merged case and asks a logical condition for one root.

matches.rationale: Both compare differently written exact numbers by translating a logarithm into a bound between successive powers of its base and comparing to simple exact benchmarks. The original additionally needs a GP sum and conjugate/nested-surds; the candidate adds exact trig values and a power of a base between zero and one.
sharedKnowledge: Both compare differently written exact numbers by translating a logarithm into a bound between successive powers of its base and comparing to simple exact benchmarks. The original additionally needs a GP sum and conjugate/nested-surds; the candidate adds exact trig values and a power of a base between zero and one.

matches.rationale: Both recognise a nested surd as a binomial square and check the sign of its square root before exact comparison or simplification. The original compares that value with several other forms, including a conjugate-rationalised surd; the candidate simplifies a sum of two nested radicals.
sharedKnowledge: Both recognise a nested surd as a binomial square and check the sign of its square root before exact comparison or simplification. The original compares that value with several other forms, including a conjugate-rationalised surd; the candidate simplifies a sum of two nested radicals.

matches.rationale: Both apply horizontal transformations in two different orders, equate the resulting functions and rename an input to prove an all-real periodic identity in both directions. The original includes a horizontal stretch and a right shift; the candidate swaps only reflection and a left shift.
sharedKnowledge: Both apply horizontal transformations in two different orders, equate the resulting functions and rename an input to prove an all-real periodic identity in both directions. The original includes a horizontal stretch and a right shift; the candidate swaps only reflection and a left shift.

matches.rationale: Both compose a translation, reflection and horizontal stretch in the stated order and invert the horizontal scale in the function argument. The candidate obtains one transformed quadratic; the original compares two orders for a general function to obtain an identity.
sharedKnowledge: Both compose a translation, reflection and horizontal stretch in the stated order and invert the horizontal scale in the function argument. The candidate obtains one transformed quadratic; the original compares two orders for a general function to obtain an identity.

matches.rationale: Both turn a two-variable reciprocal equation into a complete count of positive integer pairs using denominator restrictions and a finite divisibility search. The original completes a shifted-factor product; the candidate first derives the reciprocal relation from polygon angles and its current teaching bounds one variable before enumerating. The official alternative also uses shifted-factor completion, but that is not claimed to be its current hint route.
sharedKnowledge: Both turn a two-variable reciprocal equation into a complete count of positive integer pairs using denominator restrictions and a finite divisibility search. The original completes a shifted-factor product; the candidate first derives the reciprocal relation from polygon angles and its current teaching bounds one variable before enumerating. The official alternative also uses shifted-factor completion, but that is not claimed to be its current hint route.

matches.rationale: Both factor a two-parameter quadratic inequality, keep both sign regions and identify wedges bounded by two lines. The candidate obtains the condition from a quadratic discriminant with p>0; the original obtains it from a derivative and additionally clips to a square and measures area.
sharedKnowledge: Both factor a two-parameter quadratic inequality, keep both sign regions and identify wedges bounded by two lines. The candidate obtains the condition from a quadratic discriminant with p>0; the original obtains it from a derivative and additionally clips to a square and measures area.

matches.rationale: Both test each proposed side/diagonal/angle condition separately as a guarantee of a stronger quadrilateral shape and verify counterexamples inside the stated class. The candidate begins with parallelograms and targets squares; the original allows all convex quadrilaterals, targets rhombi and adds similarity/congruence conditions.
sharedKnowledge: Both test each proposed side/diagonal/angle condition separately as a guarantee of a stronger quadrilateral shape and verify counterexamples inside the stated class. The candidate begins with parallelograms and targets squares; the original allows all convex quadrilaterals, targets rhombi and adds similarity/congruence conditions.

matches.rationale: Both construct exact quadrilaterals with perpendicular diagonals and check whether additional symmetry or equal-side conclusions are forced. The candidate also examines the side-midpoint quadrilateral; the original additionally distinguishes equal-area and congruent-triangle conditions.
sharedKnowledge: Both construct exact quadrilaterals with perpendicular diagonals and check whether additional symmetry or equal-side conclusions are forced. The candidate also examines the side-midpoint quadrilateral; the original additionally distinguishes equal-area and congruent-triangle conditions.

matches.rationale: Both test whether separate triangle conditions force congruence, using similarity plus a size constraint and allowed supplementary-angle counterexamples. The candidate uses equal area to fix scale; the original uses equal hypotenuses after proving right angles and must handle a swapped leg correspondence within a quadrilateral.
sharedKnowledge: Both test whether separate triangle conditions force congruence, using similarity plus a size constraint and allowed supplementary-angle counterexamples. The candidate uses equal area to fix scale; the original uses equal hypotenuses after proving right angles and must handle a swapped leg correspondence within a quadrilateral.
